about: The compounds for the compound challenge: real AI systems made by combining elements.

compounds.name: Grounded Assistant
compounds.what: A chatbot that looks up trusted documents before it answers, so its replies are based on real sources rather than memory alone.
compounds.example: A school helpdesk bot that answers staff questions straight from the policy handbook.
compounds.loop: A person keeps the documents up to date and spot-checks the answers.
compounds.debate: Should a school chatbot answer parents’ questions without a member of staff checking?

compounds.name: General Chatbot
compounds.what: A chat window on top of a large language model, built on the transformer. It predicts the most likely next words, which is why it can sound sure even when it is wrong.
compounds.example: Asking a chatbot to explain photosynthesis in simpler words.
compounds.loop: You check anything that matters against a trusted source before you rely on it.
compounds.debate: Should students have to say when they have used a chatbot for homework?

compounds.name: Safe Study Buddy
compounds.what: An LLM chatbot with guardrails, designed to coach students rather than do the work for them.
compounds.example: A tutor bot that offers hints and questions instead of full answers.
compounds.loop: Teachers set the rules and review how it is being used.
compounds.debate: Should AI tutors give students answers, or only hints?

compounds.name: Fake Citation
compounds.what: A language model confidently inventing sources, quotes or facts that do not exist.
compounds.example: An essay with references to books and articles that were never written.
compounds.loop: Check every source yourself before you use it.
compounds.debate: When AI gets a fact wrong, who is responsible: the tool or the person who used it?

compounds.name: Step-by-Step Tutor
compounds.what: A reasoning model that writes out its working in steps before it answers, so you can check each step. The steps shown are not always how it really reached the answer.

marks.Ct: writes out its working in steps

compounds.example: Getting a hint for the next line of an equation, rather than the answer.
compounds.loop: You check each step and do the working yourself.
compounds.debate: If AI can show every step, does it matter whether you can do it alone?

compounds.name: AI Search Summary
compounds.what: An AI-written answer at the top of search results, built from the pages it retrieves. Generative engine optimisation is how websites try to be part of it.

marks.Rg: built from the pages it retrieves

compounds.example: Searching a homework question and getting a summary before any links.
compounds.loop: You open the sources it used and check they say what the summary claims.
compounds.debate: If fewer people click through to websites, who will keep writing them?

compounds.name: LLM Factory
compounds.what: The recipe for a large language model: a transformer trained on vast amounts of text tokens using huge numbers of GPUs.
compounds.example: How a chatbot is built long before you type your first prompt.
compounds.loop: People choose the training data and test the result.
compounds.debate: Should we have the right to know what data an AI was trained on?

compounds.name: Supervised Agent
compounds.what: An agent that uses tools to get work done, but pauses for human approval before anything important happens.
compounds.example: An agent that drafts a school trip plan and booking, then waits for a teacher to approve it.
compounds.loop: A human signs off every consequential action.
compounds.debate: Which decisions should an AI agent never make without asking first?

compounds.name: Unchecked Agent
compounds.what: An agent given tools and full autonomy, acting without anyone checking what it does.
compounds.example: An agent with access to your email that replies to people and buys things on its own.
compounds.loop: None, and that is the risk. Swap Autonomy (Au) for Human-in-the-Loop (Hi) to stabilise it.
compounds.debate: If an AI agent makes a costly mistake, who is responsible?

compounds.name: Personal Assistant Agent
compounds.what: An agent connected to your apps that plans tasks and remembers your preferences over time.
compounds.example: An assistant that manages your calendar, drafts emails and learns your routines.
compounds.loop: You decide what it can access and what it is allowed to remember.
compounds.debate: Should an AI assistant remember things about you automatically, or only when you switch memory on?

compounds.name: Digital Errand Runner
compounds.what: An agent that operates a web browser like a person to complete online tasks.
compounds.example: Comparing train tickets and filling in the booking form for you.
compounds.loop: You confirm before it pays for or submits anything.
compounds.debate: Would you let an AI spend your money?

compounds.name: Agent Team
compounds.what: Specialised agents coordinated by an orchestrator, passing work between each other.
compounds.example: One agent researches, another writes and a third fact-checks a report.
compounds.loop: A person sets the goal and signs off the final output.
compounds.debate: If agents check each other’s work, do we still need a human checker?

compounds.name: AI Pair Programmer
compounds.what: A coding agent that builds software from plain-language requests, with tests to check the result.
compounds.example: Building a revision quiz app just by describing what it should do.
compounds.loop: A developer reviews, tests and understands the code before it ships.
compounds.debate: If AI writes the code, which coding skills still need to stay human?

compounds.name: AI Art Generator
compounds.what: A diffusion model that turns text prompts into images, raising real questions about who owns the result.
compounds.example: Creating poster artwork for the school play from a written description.
compounds.loop: A person directs, selects and edits the image, and credits the AI honestly.
compounds.debate: If AI made the picture from your prompt, who really made it?

compounds.name: Labelled AI Image
compounds.what: An AI-generated picture carrying a hidden watermark or attached content credentials, so tools can check later that it was AI-made. These signals can sometimes be stripped out.
compounds.example: A social media app adding an “AI-generated” label to a picture.
compounds.loop: Creators label their work honestly, and platforms check for the watermark.
compounds.debate: Should every AI-made image have to carry a label?

compounds.name: Voice Clone
compounds.what: Generative AI that copies a real person’s voice from a short recording. The same technology can help or harm: it depends on consent and on who is in control.
compounds.example: Harm: scam calls that imitate a family member asking urgently for money. Help: people losing their voice to illness recording it first, so they can keep speaking in their own voice.
compounds.loop: Only clone a voice with its owner’s consent. Agree a family “safe word” and check by another route before acting on an urgent call.
compounds.debate: Voice cloning can scam a family or give someone their voice back. Should it be banned, or controlled?

compounds.name: AI Call Translator
compounds.what: Translates what you say during a call and speaks it in the other language, in a synthetic copy of your own voice, made with your consent.

marks.Ts: speaks it in the other language
marks.Ga: synthetic copy of your own voice

compounds.example: A parent phoning school in Polish, and staff hearing them in English, in the parent’s own voice.
compounds.loop: The speaker agrees to their voice being copied, and the call makes clear the voice is AI-translated.
compounds.debate: If a copy of your voice is made with your consent, is it still a deepfake? What makes the difference?

compounds.name: Viral Fake Video
compounds.what: Realistic AI video of something that never happened, mass-produced to spread on social media.
compounds.example: A fake clip of a celebrity or politician saying something they never said.
compounds.loop: Pause and check where a video came from before you share it, and report fakes.
compounds.debate: Should platforms remove deepfakes, or just label them?

compounds.name: Social Media Feed
compounds.what: A recommendation engine that predicts what you are most likely to watch or click, and shows you more of it.

marks.Pa: predicts what you are most likely to watch or click

compounds.example: The “For you” page on a video app.
compounds.loop: You tell it what you are not interested in, and choose when to scroll away.
compounds.debate: Do you choose what you watch, or does the app?

compounds.name: Filter Bubble
compounds.what: A recommendation engine that keeps showing you more of what you already watch or agree with, so you see fewer different views. Its picks lean towards whatever keeps you watching.
compounds.example: A video feed that can drift towards more extreme content.
compounds.loop: Users can reset or switch off personalisation, and platforms audit their feeds for harm.
compounds.debate: Should social media apps let you turn the algorithm off?

compounds.name: Automated CV Screener
compounds.what: A classifier that reads job applications and sorts candidates, and can inherit bias from past hiring decisions.
compounds.example: Software that ranks applicants before any person reads their application.
compounds.loop: A person reviews rejections and audits the results for unfair patterns.
compounds.debate: Should AI decide who gets a job interview?

compounds.name: Accountable Decision System
compounds.what: A predictive system that explains its reasoning, is checked for fairness and keeps a person in charge.
compounds.example: An appeals tool where every decision can be explained, challenged and overturned.
compounds.loop: A named person can review and overturn any decision.
compounds.debate: Do you have a right to know why an AI decided something about you?

compounds.name: Customer Service Bot
compounds.what: A chatbot that uses sentiment analysis to notice when a customer is getting upset, and hands them over to a person.

marks.Hi: hands them over to a person

compounds.example: An online shop’s help chat passing you to a human when it cannot sort out a refund.
compounds.loop: A trained member of staff takes over the difficult conversations.
compounds.debate: Should companies always tell you whether you are talking to a bot or a person?

compounds.name: Spam Filter
compounds.what: A classifier trained on labelled examples of junk mail, which sorts new emails into inbox or spam.
compounds.example: Phishing emails pretending to be from your school landing in the junk folder.
compounds.loop: You mark its mistakes as “spam” or “not spam”, which teaches it.
compounds.debate: Is it worse to miss a real email or to let a scam through?

compounds.name: Bank Fraud Alert
compounds.what: Anomaly detection that learns your usual spending over time, and flags payments that do not fit.
compounds.example: A text asking “Was this you?” after an unusual card payment.
compounds.loop: You confirm or deny the payment in your banking app or by calling the number on your card, never through a link in a text, and the bank investigates.
compounds.debate: How much should a bank know about how you spend your money?

compounds.name: Accidental Data Leak
compounds.what: Private information pasted into an AI tool that has not been approved, where it may be stored or used for training.

marks.Sh: AI tool that has not been approved

compounds.example: Copying a class list with names and grades into a free chatbot to tidy it up.
compounds.loop: Use only approved tools, and remove names and personal details first.
compounds.debate: Should schools ban free AI tools, or teach people to use them safely?

compounds.name: Jailbreak-Resistant Chatbot
compounds.what: A chatbot whose guardrails have been tested against jailbreak attempts by red teams, and strengthened where they failed.
compounds.example: A company inviting testers to try to trick its chatbot before launch.
compounds.loop: Safety teams keep testing and fixing it after release.
compounds.debate: Should companies be allowed to release a chatbot before independent testers have checked its safety rules?

compounds.name: AI Safety Lab
compounds.what: Testing, attacking and measuring a model before release to find and fix harmful behaviour.
compounds.example: Red teamers trying to trick a chatbot into giving dangerous advice, so it can be fixed.
compounds.loop: People set the standards a model must meet before release.
compounds.debate: Who should decide whether an AI model is safe enough to release?

compounds.name: Demand Forecaster
compounds.what: Predictive models that use past patterns to estimate what will be needed next.

marks.Fc: estimate what will be needed next

compounds.example: Predicting how many school lunches to cook each day to cut food waste.
compounds.loop: Staff adjust for things the data cannot know, like a trip day or a snow day.
compounds.debate: How much should we trust a prediction we cannot explain?

compounds.name: Early Warning System
compounds.what: Analytics that flag people likely to disengage or drop out, and suggest how to help.

marks.Ch: likely to disengage or drop out

compounds.example: Spotting students whose attendance patterns suggest they may need support.
compounds.loop: A trusted adult decides what, if anything, to do. The system only flags.
compounds.debate: Should schools act on AI predictions about individual students?

compounds.name: Win-Back Offer
compounds.what: Churn prediction spots who is about to cancel a subscription, so they can be sent a deal to stay.

marks.Pa: spots who is about to cancel

compounds.example: A streaming app sending you a discount after you have watched less for a few weeks, before you have even thought about cancelling.
compounds.loop: People decide which offers are fair, and you decide whether to stay.
compounds.debate: Is it fair to use AI to predict when you are about to leave?

compounds.name: Paperless Back Office
compounds.what: Documents are scanned, read and entered into systems automatically, with no retyping.
compounds.example: Invoices and permission slips processed straight into school systems.
compounds.loop: Staff handle the exceptions the system flags as unclear.
compounds.debate: Which school admin jobs should be automated, and which should not?

compounds.name: No-Code Workflow
compounds.what: A visual automation where one event triggers actions across several apps.
compounds.example: A form submission that updates a spreadsheet and emails a confirmation automatically.
compounds.loop: A person designs the flow and checks it whenever something changes.
compounds.debate: Should everyone learn to build automations, not just programmers?

compounds.name: Hyperautomated Office
compounds.what: Process mining finds the work worth automating, and digital workers take it on across the organisation.
compounds.example: An organisation mapping its processes and handing repetitive steps to bots.
compounds.loop: People redesign roles and keep the judgement calls.
compounds.debate: If digital workers take on routine tasks, what should people do with the time?

compounds.name: Smart Speaker
compounds.what: A virtual assistant that listens, works out what you mean and talks back.
compounds.example: Asking for a timer, the weather or a song while you cook.
compounds.loop: You choose where it sits, when the microphone is on and what it can control.
compounds.debate: Should smart speakers be allowed in classrooms?

compounds.name: Accessibility Assistant
compounds.what: A multimodal model that sees through a camera and describes the world out loud.
compounds.example: An app that reads signs and describes surroundings for blind and partially sighted people.
compounds.loop: The user decides when to rely on it and when to double-check.
compounds.debate: If an app describing the world for a blind person sometimes gets it wrong, should it still be used? Who is responsible for its mistakes?

compounds.name: Live Translator
compounds.what: A tool that turns speech or text in one language into another language and reads it out loud.
compounds.example: A new student and their family talking with school staff in two languages.
compounds.loop: A professional translator checks anything important, such as medical or legal information.
compounds.debate: Will AI translation mean fewer people learn languages? Is that a loss?

compounds.name: Face Unlock
compounds.what: A neural network that recognises your face, running on the device so the image never has to leave it.
compounds.example: Unlocking a phone by looking at it.
compounds.loop: You choose whether to switch it on, and keep a passcode as a back-up.
compounds.debate: Should schools use face recognition for lunch payments or registration?

compounds.name: On-Device AI
compounds.what: A small, fine-tuned model that runs on your own phone, so your data does not have to leave the device.
compounds.example: Predictive text and photo search that work even when you are offline.
compounds.loop: You control the device and what it is allowed to do.
compounds.debate: Is AI on your phone more trustworthy than AI in the cloud?

compounds.name: Self-Driving Car
compounds.what: Computer vision to see the road, machine learning trained on millions of miles of recorded and simulated driving, and edge AI to decide in a split second on board.
compounds.example: Robotaxis in some cities, and lane-keeping and emergency braking in ordinary cars.
compounds.loop: Safety drivers, remote operators and regulators decide where it may drive.
compounds.debate: If a self-driving car crashes, who is to blame?

compounds.name: Robot Vacuum
compounds.what: Sees the room, plans a route and adjusts on board as it goes.
compounds.example: A robot vacuum mapping a house and steering around furniture.
compounds.loop: You set no-go zones and decide whether its map of your home is shared.
compounds.debate: Which household jobs would you hand to a robot, and which would you not?

compounds.name: Game-Playing Champion
compounds.what: Reinforcement learning at huge scale, discovering strategies through millions of practice games.
compounds.example: AlphaGo, which learned partly by playing millions of games against itself, beating Go world champion Lee Sedol in 2016.
compounds.loop: Humans design the goals and the rewards the system learns from.
compounds.debate: If AI can beat us at a game, is the game still worth playing?

compounds.name: AI Data Centre
compounds.what: Buildings full of AI chips that power cloud AI, using large amounts of electricity and water.

marks.Sl: large amounts of electricity and water

compounds.example: The hidden infrastructure behind every chatbot reply and generated image.
compounds.loop: Companies and policymakers decide where to build and how to report the impact.
compounds.debate: Should AI companies have to publish their energy and water use?

compounds.name: Confident but Wrong
compounds.what: A chatbot giving an answer that sounds sure of itself but is made up.
compounds.example: A helper app tells you a “fact” about your town that isn’t true.
compounds.loop: You check it in a book, on a trusted website or with an adult.
compounds.debate: How can you tell when a chatbot might be making something up?

compounds.name: What to Watch Next
compounds.what: An algorithm that suggests videos or songs based on what you watched before.
compounds.example: The row of videos that appears after the one you just finished.
compounds.loop: You choose what to watch, and when to stop.
compounds.debate: Should an app choose what you watch next, or should you?

compounds.name: Voice Helper
compounds.what: A virtual assistant that listens to your question and talks back out loud.
compounds.example: Asking a speaker in the kitchen what the weather will be.
compounds.loop: A grown-up decides what it can do and when it can listen.
compounds.debate: Should a voice helper always be listening? Why, or why not?

compounds.name: Photo Sorter
compounds.what: AI that looks at photos and sorts them by what is in them.
compounds.example: A phone gathering all your photos of dogs into one album.
compounds.loop: You move a photo when it ends up in the wrong place.
compounds.debate: What might a photo sorter get wrong, and why?

compounds.name: Picture Maker
compounds.what: AI that makes a picture from the words you type.

marks.Ti: makes a picture from the words you type

compounds.example: Typing “a cat in a spacesuit” and getting a brand-new picture.
compounds.loop: With your teacher, using a school-approved tool: you decide if it is any good, and say it was made with AI.
compounds.debate: If AI made the picture, who is the artist?

compounds.name: Think Before You Share
compounds.what: Typing private things, like your address or a password, into a chatbot.
compounds.example: Telling a chatbot your full name and which school you go to.
compounds.loop: Ask a trusted adult before you share anything personal online.
compounds.debate: What should you never tell a chatbot?

compounds.name: Teaching a Computer
compounds.what: A computer learning from lots of examples, instead of being told the rules.
compounds.example: Showing a computer hundreds of pictures of apples until it can spot one on its own.
compounds.loop: People choose the examples and check what it has learned.
compounds.debate: What would go wrong if every example apple was red?

compounds.name: Human in Charge
compounds.what: AI that suggests an answer, with a person who checks it and makes the final choice.
compounds.example: A teacher reading an AI’s marking suggestions before giving out marks.
compounds.loop: A person always has the final say.
compounds.debate: Which decisions should always be made by a person?
